A B S T R A C T
In the present study, pool boiling heat transfer experiments are performed on a bare copper surface, a
sandblasted copper surface, and carbon nanotube coated copper substrates. Experiments were conducted on the substrate surface area of 14 × 14 mm2 using de-mineralized water as the working fluid.
The substrate is fixed tightly on the heater block, which is embedded with six cartridge heaters of total
capacity 1500 W. Heat fluxes were measured using J-type thermocouples, which were aligned vertically along the heater block and also 1 mm from the top of the substrate. The pool boiling heat transfer
experiments were conducted on bare, sandblasted and vertically aligned CNT coated copper substrates.
The obtained results of sandblasted and CNT coated surfaces were compared with that of the bare copper
surface. A remarkable enhancement of 38% in the CHF was observed on the CNT coated surface. The CNT
coated surface was found to be effective in increasing the nucleate boiling and the CHF.

1. Introduction
Heat transfer enhancement is the one of the major concerns in
heat exchangers and micro electro mechanical system (MEMS). The
recent advancements in technology have contributed to a tremendous size reduction of electronic devices, which has led to a high
heat flux. So, the cooling of these devices has become a challenging task. Among the different heat transfer techniques in electronic
devices and microprocessors, pool boiling is an effective method due
to its change of phase. Different passive techniques are used to
enhance heat transfer such as increase of sub cooling, increase of
surface roughness by surface modification and surface coating [1].
Among the different passive techniques, surface coating is an effi-
cient method to improve the heat transfer characteristics by
increasing the effective heat transfer area, nucleation density, bubble
frequency and wettability [2-5].

Surface coatings can be macro-structured, micro-structured, and
nano-structured; among them, nano-structured coatings have potential application in MEMS devices. Nano-structured coating
possesses the following desired properties: high surface area to
volume ratio, smaller volume and mass, and high convective heat
transfer coefficient; these causes the removal of large amounts of
heat flux. Porosity, fin action and surface roughness of the
nanostructured coating are the major parameters which enhances
the heat transfer [6-13]. Extensive research has been carried out
on pool boiling using surface coating. Ahn et al. conducted flow
boiling and pool boiling analyses on different metallic substrates
coated with TiO2, SiO2 and Ag nano particles. For pool boiling and
flow boiling, a significant increase in the critical heat flux (CHF) was
recorded for all coated surfaces. The enhancement of CHF on coated
surfaces is mainly due to change in wettability and capillarity which
increase liquid spreading and actively supplied cooling water to the
heating surface. Sujith Kumar et al. [14] conducted the flow boiling
heat transfer experiments and found that 21.6% of CHF was enhanced at the flux rate of 283 kg/m2s over carbon nanotubes with
diamond coating acting as intermediate layer on a copper sub-
strate for the demineralized water as a working fluid. Similar kind
of surface coating was thought to be effective in case of pool boiling
and is tried in this work. The investigation may lead to some deeper
insights into the actual performance of vertically aligned CNTs for
the enhancement of phase change heat transfer. This was the drive
behind this investigation in the case of pool boiling heat transfer
leading to applications like electronics cooling. Mudawar and Anderson [3] found out a pool boiling augmentation on finned and
microstudded surfaces. These surfaces are more effective to enhance
the CHF due to increase in surface area with a mild increase in the
fin volume. Ahn et al. [6] conducted pool boiling experiments on
CNT coated silicon substrates. Experiments were conducted on bare
silicon wafer and two silicon wafers, each deposited with a uniform
layer of vertically aligned MWCNTs of different heights of 9 μm and
25 μm respectively. A maximum enhancement of 40% in CHF was
obtained for the 25 μm height CNT coated surface. Ujereh et al. [4]
conducted pool boiling experiments for assessing the impact of CNT
coating on both copper and silicon substrates. Experiments were
conducted using FC-72 as the working fluid. They obtained 35% of
enhancement in CHF for the coated substrate than for the bare
substrates.
The recent advances in nanotechnology have led to the development of carbon nanotube (CNT) coatings over metallic substrates,
which are the most efficient way to remove the high heat flux from
small areas. Pathak et al. [15] coated the CNT fins over the shape
memory alloy wire, and conducted a study on heat transfer. They
found an appreciable enhancement in the cooling rate of the CNT
coated wire compared to the uncoated one. The enhancement in
the cooling rate was due to the high thermal conductivity of the
CNT and increase in the total heat transfer area.
Jean-Marc Bonard et al. [16] stated that a major problem for CNT
coatings with the metallic substrate is the poor adhesion between
the CNT and the substrate, which will increase the intermediate re-
sistance. Extensive research is being carried out to overcome this
problem. The adhesion between the metal and the CNT can be increased by using an intermediate layer. Kumar et al. [17] used omega
bond gluing agent as an intermediate layer to increase the adhesion between the CNT and the stainless steel substrate. Song et al.
[18] reported that adding a thin layer of indium improved the adhesion between the CNT arrays and the substrate. Khanikar et al.
[19] conducted a flow boiling heat transfer studies on CNT coated
copper substrates. They prepared the CNT coating over the copper
substrate, with a tri-layer of titanium, aluminium and iron as the
intermediate metal catalysts. The titanium layer gives high bonding
strength for the CNT, the aluminium layer was used for segregating the annealed iron nano particles, and the iron layer acts as a
catalyst for the CNT growth. Lin et al. [20] used the Al2O3 intermediate layer as a thermal interface material to coat the vertically
aligned CNTs on the copper substrate.
In the present work, to improve the adhesion between the CNTs
and the Cu substrate, a diamond intermediate layer was coated
between the CNTs and the copper. Furthermore, to enhance the adhesion between the diamond layer and the copper substrate, a
diamond layer deposition was achieved on a sandblasted copper sub-
strate. The hot filament chemical vapour deposition technique is used
for coating the diamond and the CNT. Pool boiling heat transfer
studies were conducted on the CNT coated copper substrate, bare
copper and sand blasted copper substrate.
2. Experiment
2.1. Double-layered structure deposition
The oxygen-free copper substrate was etched with HNO3 and HCl,
and then ultrasonic cleaning was carried out in a bath containing
99% ethanol for 30 minutes. The cleaned copper substrate was sandblasted for 1 minute, and prepared for the HFCVD deposition. Copper
substrate was first ultrasonically seeded in a suspension of ethanol
and nano-size diamond powders, and placed in the HFCVD chamber
for the deposition. The precursor gases are CH4 (2 vol. %) and H2 (98
vol. %) with a total flow rate of 50 sccm and the pressure inside the
chamber was maintained at 20 torr at 400 °C substrate back temperature. For CNTs growth: a ferric nitrate catalyst was coated on
the diamond layer by spin coating, and the spin coating time was
set at 30 seconds. A dc-bias voltage of -500 V and a glow discharge current of 100 mA was supplied to assist the CNT alignment
growth in a CH4 (20 vol. %) and H2 (80 vol. %), with a gas mixture
of total gas flow rate of 50 sccm.
2.2. Details of characterization equipment
The surface morphology of the Cu substrate and diamond coatings was observed using SEM (JSM-6010). The surface roughness
was measured by MitatoyoSuftest (ISO 1997 standard, cut off length
20 mm, resolution: 0.0001 μm). The phase analysis was done by the
Raman Microscope (Renishaw 2000) and XRD (RigakuGeigerflex
XRD). Static contact angle of the surface was measured by contact
angle metre (Holmarc, HO-IAD-CAM-01A).
2.3. Experimental apparatus
The constructional details of the experimental setup used in this
study are shown in Fig. 1. The experimental setup consists of the
following components: 1) a viewing chamber, 2) test plate 3) heating
block, 4) auxiliary heater, 5) reflux condenser, 6) insulation, 7) pressure transducer, 8) data logger and j type thermocouples are used
where temperatures to be measured and the viewing chamber are
made of acrylic enclosure. The copper test plate is heated by using
six cartridge heaters with a capacity of 250 W each. The rate of heat
is controlled by an autotransformer of the range of 0-2000 W. An
auxiliary heater was provided for controlling the fluid bulk temperature, and a water cooled condenser is used for condensing the
vapour produced during the pool boiling process. A thick layer of
glass wool insulation was provided for reducing the heat loss to the
surroundings. Heat loss in the radial direction in the heater block
was analyzed using COMSOL multiphysics software and was found
to be negligible. This result was well expected as the heater block
was well insulated radially using Teflon and glass wool, thus minimizing the heat loss to negligible values. Three J type thermocouples
were inserted at 1 mm below the top surface of the copper sub-
strate for measuring the surface temperatures along the length of
the substrate and two J type thermocouples were inserted 4 mm

The experimental uncertainty for the wall heat flux and boiling

2.6. Experimental procedure
Pool boiling experiments were conducted by using de-mineralized
water. Prior to the experiment, the water was boiled vigorously for
30 minutes to remove the dissolved gases. The bulk temperature
of the water was maintained constant by using an auxiliary heater.
The heat was supplied to the testing plate in small increments by
six electrical cartridge heaters inserted in a copper block. Once the
temperature in the copper block reached the steady state, all the
temperature data from the thermocouples were recorded by using
a data logger. After all the measurements were taken, the heat flux
of the testing plate was increased, and the measurement procedure was repeated. The experiment was repeated for different values
of heat flux until the CHF is encountered which can be identified
by an abnormal rise in the surface temperature [6].

3. Result and discussion
3.1. Characterization of the coating
Fig. 2 shows the SEM image of the surface morphology of untreated (A) and sandblasted (B) Cu substrate. It can be observed that
the surface roughness has significantly increased after sandblasting. The surface roughness measurement results in Table 1 can prove
it. Fig. 3 shows the SEM image of diamond coatings on untreated
Cu substrate (A) and sandblasted Cu substrate (B). The diamond coatings were partly peeled off from the untreated Cu substrate and were
stayed on sand blasted Cu substrate. Diamond and Cu have a large
thermal expansion mismatch. When a diamond coated on Cu cools
down from a higher deposition temperature, the Cu substrate shrinks
a lot while diamond has much less contractions [21]. In the case
of a diamond coating on the bare copper surface, a high stress will
occur between these two layers and will result in cracks in the
diamond coatings. Part of the diamond coating may peel off from
the substrate due to the high stress and low affinity between
diamond and Cu [14]. In Fig. 3(A), some cracks formed on the
diamond coatings on the bare Cu substrate can be observed. These
cracks also resulted from the stress between diamond coatings and
the Cu substrate. On comparing SEM images of the diamond coating
on the bare and the sandblasted copper, we can infer that the sandblasting treatment improved the adhesion between the diamond
and the Cu substrate. This is due to mechanical interlocking between
copper surface and diamond coating [14].
Fig. 4 shows the XRD patterns of the samples presented in Fig. 3.
The diamond and Cu have a similar crystal lattice and their main
XRD diffraction peaks are very close [22]. The peaks at 50.1°, 59.7°
and 89.1° are the diffractions from the (111), (200), and (220) patterns of Cu. The diamond diffraction pattern is weak in the untreated
Cu substrate because some of them peel off, and reduce the diffraction intensity. Comparing the untreated to the sandblasted
sample, the left shift of the diamond [111] pattern and [220] pattern
is because of the stress between the diamond and Cu substrate.
Fig. 5(A and B) shows the SEM images of the CNT coated Cu sub-
strates with and without the diamond intermediate layer. The growth
of CNT is controlled by the sputtering time of catalyst preparation
and the deposition time of the CNT. The vertically aligned CNTs were
achieved by a DC-plasma hot filament CVD process. In the present
coated sample, the catalyst's spinning time and deposition time are
limited to 90 seconds and 20 minutes respectively. The length and
diameter of the CNT coatings can be measured with a highly magnified image as 300-500 nm and 50 nm respectively. Tap water flow
test is conducted to find CNT adhesion on copper substrate with a
mass flow rate of 10 l/min and the distance between tap and the

3.3. Pool boiling heat transfer studies
Pool boiling experiments were conducted with an initial bulk
temperature of de-mineralized water at 90 °C. The pool boiling heat
flux data of CNT coated Cu and sand blasted Cu were compared
with that of the bare Cu. During the experimentation, we found
that the commencement of nucleation for the CNT coated surface
and sand blasted surface occurred at a lower surface temperature
and lower heat flux as compared to that of the bare copper surface.
The nucleation sites for the CNT coated surface were more due to
its higher relative roughness compared to the sand blasted copper.
The higher nucleation density will lead to an early onset of boiling;
thereby, wall superheat of the sand blasted surface decreases for
corresponding heat flux considered with the bare copper surface.
Larger heat fluxes were obtained from the sand blasted copper and
CNT coated surface with respect to wall superheat. The transition
from nucleate to film boiling over sand blasted copper and bare
copper is rapid compared to the CNT coated surface. In the case of
the CNT coated surface, the initial bubble density was higher due
to its higher surface roughness, but its hydrophobicity slowed down
the growth of the formed bubbles. At higher heat flux, the bubbles
spread over the surface, causing coalescence [5], which leads to a
slow transition from nucleate to film boiling. Another major reason
for the increase in the bubble nucleation over the CNT coated surface
is the protruding nanostructures. This in turn increases the effective surface area near the wall, leading to increase in the nucleation
sites.
3.4. Heat flux data
The amount of heat flux supplied to the water using the copper
heating block was calculated using Eqn. (1). Fig. 8 shows the saturated pool boiling curves for the three different surfaces (bare copper
surface, sandblasted copper surface, and CNT-coated surface). The
data were obtained from the average of the temperature measurements at the three thermocouple locations and the initial bulk
temperature of the fluid.
The shapes of the boiling curves for all the above mentioned surfaces were almost the same but a leftward temperature shift occurred
in the case of the CNT coated surface for different heat fluxes. From
the boiling curves, we can infer that in the CNT coated surface the

wall superheat is less than that of the other two samples for all the
measured conditions. This anomalous behaviour is due to hydrophobicity, fin action, increasing surface area and high relative surface
roughness. For the sandblasted copper, in a low heat flux region,
there is a reduction in the wall superheat and this effect was close
enough to CNT coated sample. Close to the critical heat flux region,
the wall superheat of the bare copper and sand blasted copper is
almost same. In the case of sand blasted copper, due to its higher

hike in CHF was also found due to the higher heat transfer area. It
is observed that the CNT coated surface enhances the heat flux in
the nucleate boiling regime by 48%, and that of sand blasted copper
is 12%, with respect to the bare copper surface.
3.5. Critical heat flux
Table 3 shows the variation of the critical heat flux and surface
roughness of different tested samples. Both the CNT coated surface
and sand blasted surface shows an enhancement in the CHF with
respect to the bare copper surface. The enhancement in the CHF compared to bare copper, for the sand blasted copper, is around 8.5%

and that of CNT coating is 38%. From Table 1, we can compare the
surface roughness of all the three surfaces. The CNT coated surface
gives a maximum increase in the surface roughness, compared to
other two surfaces.
CNTs maintained in a vertical direction not only increase the
surface area but also increase the fin effectiveness (nano-fin
effect) because copper substrate has lower thermal conductivity
than the axial thermal conductivity of individual vertically aligned
CNTs.
AHN et al. [6] suggested that nano fin effect caused to enhance
local quenching of the heater surface due to which an increment
in the CHF takes place in the vertically aligned CNTs coated surface.
The surface roughness of the sand blasted surface is higher than that
of the bare copper surface. An increase in the surface roughness increases the total area for heat transfer which will enhance the CHF
of the coated surface as compared to the bare surface.
3.6. Boiling heat transfer coefficient
The effective heat transfer coefficient is calculated using Eqn. (2)
up to the critical heat flux. Fig. 9 presents the variation of the boiling
heat transfer coefficient with heat flux, for three different samples.
The CNT coatings show a very large enhancement in the heat transfer coefficient compared to the other two samples. The maximum
increase of 80% in heat transfer coefficient is obtained from the CNT
coated surface compared to the bare copper surface. The higher heat
transfer coefficient of the CNT coated surface is due to its high surface
roughness, effective heat transfer area and Nano fin effect. The use
of an intermediate diamond coating reduces the intermediate re-
sistance of the CNT coating over the copper surface by increasing
the adhesion. The diamond provides the carbon bonding between
the CNT and copper. A reduction in the intermediate resistance leads
to a higher heat transfer rate by maintaining a constant temperature between the top surface and the tip of the fin. For the sand
blasted copper sample, the boiling heat transfer coefficient is slightly
higher than that of the bare Cu due to its higher surface roughness. An increase in the surface roughness increases the effective
surface area for heat transfer which in turn increases the heat transfer rate from the surface.

3.7. Wettability effects
The wetting ability of water on different surfaces is evaluated
by measuring the contact angle of the water on the surfaces. Fig. 10
shows the contact angle on the bare copper, sand blasted Cu, and
CNT coatings. It can be seen from Fig. 10 that the contact angles of
the bare copper and sand blasted copper are less than 90o; hence,
it is hydrophilic in nature. While the CNT coated surface that provides a contact angle of 133° is hydrophobic. The hydrophobicity
of the CNT coated surface is due to the combined effect of diamond
intermediate and CNT coating. The wettability is the highest for the
bare Cu and the lowest for the CNT coatings. Boiling begins earlier

As the heat flux increases, the bubble density increases, which

but this phenomenon was not occurring on the CNT coated surface.
The fin action of CNT hinders the growth of the bubbles. This action
of the fins can enhance the pool boiling heat transfer characteristics of the CNT coated surface in the high heat flux region.
4. Conclusions
The pool boiling heat flux has been measured and analyzed on
the sandblasted Cu, CNT coated copper and bare copper surfaces
under an initial bulk temperature of de-mineralized water at 90 °C.
The key findings from the study are as follows:
1. Early onset of boiling is obtained for both the CNT and sand
blasted Cu samples compared to the bare Cu sample due to higher
nucleation density. This effect is due to the hyrophobicity and
high relative roughness for the CNT coated samples. Sand blasted
copper shows an early onset only due to the high relative
roughness.
2. The boiling behaviour is almost similar for all the tested samples.
In the case of the CNT, a leftward shift in boiling is obtained compared to the sand blasted copper and bare copper surfaces. For
the CNT coated sample, the leftward shift in the boiling curve
at low heat flux is due to high nucleation density resulting from
its hydrophobic behaviour.
In the case of the CNT coated surface, an increase and leftward
shift of the CHF are found due to the fin effect and increase in surface
area; thereby, the boiling curve of the CNT coated sample continues along the left side of the sand blasted copper curve and bare
copper curve.
For the CNT coated and sand blasted copper surfaces compared with the bare copper, an enhancement in the CHF of 38% and
8.5% respectively were obtained. An enhancement in the heat transfer coefficient of 80% and 13%, respectively, was found in the CNT
coated and sand blasted surfaces, compared with the bare copper
surface. Increases in the CHF and heat transfer coefficient are mainly
due to the increase in the effective surface area for heat transfer.
The CNT coated surface shows the better enhancement due to its
fin action, high thermal conductivity, and lower intermediate re-
sistance between the CNT and the surface with an intermediate
diamond coating.
